rv.q: They are enough for each other, and reason enough to see this “Jenufa.”
This gloomy backdrop and Mr. Guth’s astutely detailed direction made the torments of the four principal characters all the more vivid.
The evening, inevitably, was about music and singing—and there, they got things just right.

And, musically, this performance was a triumph — thanks, also, to Brno-born conductor Tomáš Hanus, in his house debut, who had a sure sense of the score’s narrative sweep and drew incisive, colourful playing from the Met Orchestra.
Don’t miss this powerful and well-cast production of an underrated masterpiece.
Under Tomáš Hanus, the Metropolitan Opera Orchestra brought out the richness of Janáček’s score, from its driving momentum to passages of unexpected lyricism.

That the highly touted production proved the most negligible part of the experience in no way detracted from the evening, which was musically and expressively as affecting as one will find at the Met this season, Jenůfa is great because it does what opera is designed to do, as well as it can be done.
The biggest issue with this production is that it looked empty and unfinished on the massive Met stage.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Grigorian's electrifying performance and Janáček's opera itself, though Guth's symbol-heavy staging divides opinion—thrilling to most, heavy-handed to some.
